flashcards.front: What is the primary threat vector for Linux Permission Controls?
flashcards.back_definition: Adversaries exploit excessive chmod 777 permissions on proprietary system binaries to bypass standard perimeter security controls.
flashcards.back_example: Example: Permissions warning: file has excessive rwxrwxrwx settings
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse this threat with other layers (like physical breaches or certificate revocations) which target different assets.
flashcards.back_hook: Recall: excessive chmod 777 permissions is the unlocked door; proprietary system binaries is what the attacker wants to steal.

flashcards.front: How does the security team mitigate Linux Permission Controls threats?
flashcards.back_definition: Deploying and enforcing chmod 700 owner-only restrictions directly hardens proprietary system binaries and blocks unauthorized connections.
flashcards.back_example: Action: Update security configurations to require chmod 700 owner-only restrictions.
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse mitigation (actively blocking the exploit) with detection (simply logging or alerting the event).
flashcards.back_hook: Mitigation is the shield; detection is the security camera.

flashcards.front: How do analysts detect exploitation of Linux Permission Controls?
flashcards.back_definition: By auditing event data and implementing logic flags built to alert on directory permission sweeps.
flashcards.back_example: Syslog trace: Permissions warning: file has excessive rwxrwxrwx settings
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse signature-based detection (matching known strings) with anomaly-based detection (mapping dynamic standard deviations).
flashcards.back_hook: Detection is looking for the fingerprint left behind by the threat.
